name: Residual Current Device (RCD)
tagline: Watches the balance between live and neutral — any leakage to earth trips it in milliseconds.
parts: Trip indicator flag — shows the pole that opened
Summation transformer — compares L and N current
Solenoid — releases the mechanism on imbalance
L, N terminals — in (top) and out (bottom)
safety: An RCD does not protect against overload — that is the MCB's job. RCD + MCB together (or one RCBO) is the standard way final circuits are built in UK boards today.

points.label: Test button 'T'
points.detail: Pressing test injects a deliberate L-to-earth imbalance and the RCD must trip. Standards (IEC/BS) require a quarterly test; press it along with the MCB lever test to confirm both poles open clean.

points.label: Trip indicator flag
points.detail: Many RCDs show a coloured window that flips to red/released when it has tripped. That tells you the trip came from earth leakage rather than someone simply switching it off.

points.label: Summation transformer
points.detail: A toroidal core passes both live and neutral. While they carry equal and opposite current the flux cancels; any imbalance (leakage via earth) produces net flux the pick-up coil senses.

points.label: Tripping solenoid
points.detail: At the rated trip current (commonly 30 mA) the sense winding energises a solenoid that releases the latch with a spring — typically in under 40 ms, quick enough to stop a lethal shock from establishing.

points.label: L / N terminals
points.detail: In (top) and out (bottom) for both poles. An RCD must be downstream of its MCB and must carry BOTH live and neutral — a single-pole 'L only' feed cannot detect a neutral-earth fault.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a residual current device showing the toroidal summation transformer, trip solenoid, latch mechanism and main contacts

cutawayPoints.label: Summation transformer
cutawayPoints.detail: A toroidal ring core with a sense winding, sitting so that both the live and the neutral conductor pass through its centre. Equal currents produce equal and opposite fields and cancel, so the winding sees nothing; any current leaking to earth unbalances them and induces a voltage — the whole device is that imbalance, amplified.

cutawayPoints.label: Conductors through the core
cutawayPoints.detail: Live and neutral both thread the ring. That is the trick worth seeing: an RCD does not measure current to earth, it compares what goes out with what comes back, so it trips on any difference above its rating — 30 mA on a socket circuit, 100 mA or more on a whole installation.

cutawayPoints.label: Trip solenoid
cutawayPoints.detail: The residual is only millivolts, so on a modern device it is amplified before it reaches the trip coil. The plunger strikes the latch and opens both poles; at rated residual a 30 mA device has to do it within 40 ms, and most manage a good deal less.

cutawayPoints.label: Trip latch
cutawayPoints.detail: The same over-centre latch the lever drives manually, held closed against a spring and released by either the solenoid or the test circuit — and when it goes, the lever does not return to OFF but stops mid-travel, which is how you tell a trip from a switch-off.

cutawayPoints.label: Main contacts
cutawayPoints.detail: Double-break contacts opening live and neutral together. Interrupting the whole supply rather than one conductor is what makes an RCD protection against electric shock rather than just against fire: the appliance is dead on both sides.

cutawayPoints.label: Test resistor
cutawayPoints.detail: The T button does not fake a fault in the electronics — it passes a real current through a resistor from the load side of one pole back to the supply side of the other, outside the ring. The transformer sees a genuine imbalance. That is why the button proves the mechanism and the wiring but proves nothing about your earth.
